nameStory: The common alder gets its name from the Old English 'alor,' meaning simply 'alder tree.' It's called 'common' because it's the most widespread alder species across Europe and has been naturalized in many parts of North America. The scientific name 'glutinosa' refers to the sticky, resinous quality of its young buds and shoots.
description: Common alder is a medium-sized deciduous tree that typically grows 20-30 feet tall in New England, though it can reach up to 98 feet in ideal conditions. It has a distinctive upright, oval-shaped crown and smooth, dark gray bark that becomes furrowed with age. The tree is easily recognized by its rounded, dark green leaves and its unusual cone-like fruits that persist through winter. Common alder is a pioneer species that loves wet feet and poor soils where other trees struggle to grow.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rounded to oval leaves with blunt or slightly notched tips and doubly-serrated (saw-toothed) edges. They feel somewhat sticky when young and stay dark green well into fall, often dropping while still green.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, woody, cone-like structures about half an inch long that start green and turn dark brown. They hang in clusters and persist through winter, rattling in the wind and releasing tiny winged seeds.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Separate male and female catkins appear in early spring before leaves emerge. Male catkins are long, yellowish, and droopy (2-4 inches), while female catkins are shorter, reddish, and upright.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth, dark gray to brownish bark that develops shallow furrows and diamond-shaped ridges as the tree matures. Young twigs are often sticky and reddish-brown.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Often grows in dense thickets or groves near water, with multiple stems from the base. Has an upright, oval crown and tends to lean toward light sources in shaded areas.

habitat: Common alder thrives in wet, poorly-drained soils along stream banks, pond edges, wetlands, and swampy areas throughout New England. You'll often find it colonizing disturbed wet sites like old beaver ponds or drainage ditches. It tolerates flooding and can grow in nutrient-poor soils thanks to its partnership with nitrogen-fixing bacteria in its roots.

seasonality.spring: Catkins appear in March-April before the leaves, with drooping yellow male catkins being quite showy. Fresh green leaves emerge shortly after, feeling sticky to the touch.
seasonality.summer: Dark green foliage provides dense shade, and small cone-like fruits develop and mature from green to brown. Look for the characteristic rounded leaves with saw-toothed edges.
seasonality.fall: Leaves often stay green late into the season and may drop while still green rather than changing color. The woody cones are fully mature and begin opening to release seeds.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the persistent dark brown cones that rattle in winter winds. Sticky, reddish-brown buds are visible, and the furrowed bark pattern is most apparent.

funFact: Common alder is nature's underwater construction expert—its wood actually gets harder and stronger when submerged in water, which is why it was used to build the foundations of Venice and many medieval European bridges that are still standing today after centuries underwater!
confusionNotes: Common alder is most easily confused with other alder species, but its cone-like fruits and rounded leaves with blunt tips help distinguish it from the more pointed leaves of gray alder. The persistent woody cones separate all alders from similar waterside trees like willows, which have fuzzy catkins but no cone-like fruits.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'European alder,' this tree has naturalized widely in New England and is now considered part of the regional flora. Don't confuse it with our native speckled alder, which is typically much smaller and shrub-like. The 'black alder' name can be confusing since there's also a completely unrelated shrub called winterberry that's sometimes called black alder.
compareHints: Common alder differs from gray alder by having more rounded leaves with blunt tips versus gray alder's more pointed, oval leaves. Smooth alder, our native species, is typically much smaller and more shrub-like, rarely exceeding 15 feet tall. Green alder is quite rare in New England and stays shrub-sized with smaller, more oval leaves that are often whitened underneath.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England alders, grey alder is distinguished by its speckled grayish bark and multi-stemmed shrubby growth habit.

Green alder stands out from its New England relatives by its greenish young bark - gray alder has consistently gray bark, common alder tends to be larger and more tree-like, and smooth alder has smoother leaf undersides and prefers warmer areas.
Compared to gray alder, smooth alder has much smoother bark and forms denser thickets in wetter locations.
